passages.t: Ten young women and the bridegroom who came late
passages.happening:
Jesus is still on the Mount of Olives, still answering the disciples' question about his coming (24:3). He tells a story about a wedding.

Ten young women take their lamps and go out to meet the bridegroom. Five are foolish and five are wise. The foolish ones take their lamps but no extra oil. The wise ones take flasks of oil as well. The bridegroom is a long time coming, and all ten get drowsy and fall asleep.

At midnight a shout goes up: “Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him!” (verse 6). The ten wake and trim their lamps. The foolish ones find their lamps are going out. They ask the wise to share. The wise say no, there may not be enough for everyone; go and buy your own. While the foolish are away buying, the bridegroom comes. Those who are ready go in with him to the wedding feast, “and the door was shut” (verse 10).

Later the others arrive and call out, “Lord, lord, open the door for us!” He answers, “Truly I tell you, I do not know you” (verse 12). Jesus ends with the point: “Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Only Matthew tells this parable. A parable is a short story that carries a lesson about God's kingdom.

A wedding in Jesus' world was a public event, often with a procession. The bridegroom and his party went to bring the bride, with music and lights, and the guests joined them to escort the couple to the feast. An old Jewish book, 1 Maccabees, tells of a great wedding where the bridegroom came out with his friends and his relatives, with drums and music, to meet the bride's party (1 Maccabees 9:37-39). The ten young women in the story are not brides. They are friends of the family, waiting to light the way.

What were their lamps like? The Greek word can mean a small clay oil lamp, or a torch: a stick wrapped in cloth soaked in oil, which burns bright but needs fresh oil often. Scholars still argue about which Jesus meant. Either way, the point is the same. A long wait used up the oil, and anyone without a spare flask was left in the dark.

Midnight was the worst hour to run out. The shops were shut. The errand to buy oil is almost comic, and that is part of the point. Some things cannot be borrowed at the last minute.

Once the door of the house was shut, the feast had begun and no one else came in. Jesus used the same picture in Luke, of a master who shuts the door and says, ‘I do not know where you are from’ (Luke 13:25). The words ‘I do not know you’ also echo the end of the Sermon on the Mount, where Jesus says to those who only called him Lord, “I never knew you” (7:23).

The early church kept this picture. A short Christian manual called the Didache, from around AD 100, ends with a warning to watch over your life and not to let your lamps go out (Didache 16.1). And a later Jewish parable, written down in the Babylonian Talmud several centuries after Jesus, tells of a king's banquet with no time set, where only the guests who were dressed and ready got in (Shabbat 153a; see the note on 22:11-14).
passages.ot:
In the Old Testament the bridegroom is often God himself, and Israel is his bride. “As a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you” (Isaiah 62:5). Through Hosea the LORD says, “I will betroth you to Me forever” (Hosea 2:19). When Jesus casts himself as the bridegroom, as he did earlier (9:15), he takes a part the prophets gave to God.

The closing line, that no one knows the day or the hour, repeats what Jesus has just said in 24:36. The parable is an answer to the question of 24:3, told as a story.
passages.hard:
Why don't the wise share their oil? It can sound selfish. But this is a parable, not a lesson in manners. The oil stands for something that cannot be handed over at the last minute. Readers have taken it in different ways: as faith, as good deeds, as love, as the Holy Spirit, as a life of real readiness. Most agree on the main point. No one can be ready on someone else's behalf. A parent cannot believe for a child, and a friend cannot borrow another friend's faithfulness.

Why do all ten fall asleep, even the wise? Jesus does not blame them for sleeping. The wait was long, and sleep is human. The difference between the two groups is not that one stayed awake. It is that one was prepared for a long wait. The bridegroom's delay matters too. Matthew's first readers were already waiting longer than they had expected for Jesus to come back. The parable tells them that a long delay is part of the story, not a sign that he is not coming.

‘I do not know you’ is a hard line. It is a warning, and it is meant to be one. But it is not meant to make a tender heart afraid. If you fear that the door is already shut on you, notice that you are still able to knock, and the same Jesus says, “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest” (11:28).
passages.asks: The foolish young women were not wicked. They were careless. They assumed there would be time later. Ask what you are putting off with God because you think there will be time later. Readiness is not anxiety. The wise slept well. They were ready because they had thought ahead, not because they never rested.

passages.t: The talents: three servants and what they did with what they were given
passages.happening:
Jesus tells a second story. A man about to travel calls his servants and puts his property in their hands. He gives one servant five talents, another two, and another one, “each according to his own ability” (verse 15). Then he leaves.

The servant with five talents puts them to work at once and gains five more. The one with two gains two more. But the one with one talent digs a hole in the ground and hides his master's money.

After a long time the master comes back to settle accounts. The first two servants show what they have gained. To each the master says the same words: “Well done, good and faithful servant! You have been faithful with a few things; I will put you in charge of many things. Enter into the joy of your master!” (verses 21 and 23).

The third servant comes and says, “Master, I knew that you are a hard man, reaping where you have not sown.” “So I was afraid and went out and hid your talent in the ground. See, you have what belongs to you” (verse 25). The master calls him wicked and lazy. If he believed that, he should at least have put the money with the bankers to earn interest. The talent is taken from him and given to the one who has ten. The worthless servant is thrown into the outer darkness.
passages.hearers:
A talent was not a coin. It was a weight of silver or gold, and as money it was worth about six thousand denarii. A denarius was a day's pay for a labourer (20:2), so one talent was something like twenty years of a worker's wages. For scale, the Jewish historian Josephus says that Herod Antipas, who ruled Galilee in Jesus' day, received two hundred talents a year from his whole territory (Antiquities 17.318). Even the servant who got one talent was trusted with a fortune.

Rich men often left property in the hands of trusted slaves or servants while they were away. Bankers sat at tables and paid interest on money left with them. The same word is used for the money-changers' tables in the temple (21:12).

Burying money was a normal way to keep it safe in a world with no locked bank vaults. Matthew himself tells of treasure hidden in a field (13:44). The Babylonian Talmud, written down centuries later, records a teacher named Samuel saying that money left in your care is properly guarded only if you bury it in the ground (Bava Metzia 42a). So the third servant did what many would have called the careful thing. That makes the master's verdict sharper. He did not want caution. He wanted his servants to use what he gave them.

Luke tells a similar parable, with ten servants and smaller sums called minas (Luke 19:11-27). The two stories share a shape: a master leaves, servants are trusted with money, he returns, and one servant who did nothing is condemned.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament says that everything a person has belongs to God first: “The earth is the LORD’s, and the fullness thereof” (Psalm 24:1). The servants in the parable own nothing. They look after what is their master's.

The Law of Moses forbade charging interest to a poor fellow Israelite: “you are not to charge him interest” (Exodus 22:25). The parable does not overturn that law or praise lending at interest. It is told from the side of a master who expects a return on his own money, and it uses that as a picture.

‘Enter into the joy of your master’ fits the hope of the Psalms: “You will fill me with joy in Your presence” (Psalm 16:11).
passages.hard:
Is this parable about making money? No. It is not a promise that God will make the faithful rich, and it is not a rule about investing. The talents are a picture. The master is Jesus, who is about to go away, and the servants are those who belong to him. Readers have taken the talents to stand for the gospel itself, for the gifts and abilities God gives, or for every opportunity to serve him. The parable cannot be used to say that wealth shows God's favour. In the very next passage Jesus says he is found among the hungry and the poor.

What about the third servant's picture of his master? He calls him ‘a hard man’ and says he was afraid. The master answers, in effect, ‘If that is what you thought, you should still have done something.’ Most readers think the master is not agreeing that he is harsh. He is judging the servant by his own words, as the master in Luke's version says outright: “I will judge you by your own words” (Luke 19:22). The first two servants did not find the master hard at all. They found joy. The third servant's trouble began with a false picture of the one he served. Fear made him bury what he was given.

A few modern readers have turned the story around and read the master as a greedy landowner and the third servant as an honest man who refused to join in. Most commentators think that reading goes against the way Matthew frames the parable, as a picture of the kingdom. It does remind readers how a story about money sounds to the poor.

‘Everyone who has will be given more’ (verse 29) is a saying Jesus used before about understanding the kingdom (13:12). It is not about bank balances. Whoever uses what God gives will be given more. Whoever buries it loses even that. The outer darkness and weeping are Matthew's usual words for being shut out of the kingdom (8:12; 22:13).
passages.asks: The servant who failed was not the one with the least. It was the one who was afraid. Ask what picture of God you carry. If you think of him as hard and grasping, you may bury what he has given you to keep from getting it wrong. The master did not ask the second servant for five talents. He asked for faithfulness with two. Ask what you have been given, small or large, and whether you are using it or hiding it.

passages.t: The sheep and the goats: “you did for Me”
passages.happening:
Jesus ends his long answer with a scene of judgment. “When the Son of Man comes in His glory, and all the angels with Him, He will sit on His glorious throne” (verse 31). All the nations are gathered before him. He separates people one from another, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats, and puts the sheep on his right and the goats on his left.

Then the King speaks to those on his right. They are blessed by his Father. They are to inherit the kingdom prepared for them “from the foundation of the world” (verse 34). The reason: “For I was hungry and you gave Me something to eat, I was thirsty and you gave Me something to drink, I was a stranger and you took Me in, I was naked and you clothed Me, I was sick and you looked after Me, I was in prison and you visited Me” (verses 35-36).

The righteous are amazed. When did we ever see you hungry, or thirsty, or a stranger, or sick, or in prison? The King answers, “Truly I tell you, whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me” (verse 40).
passages.hearers:
Only Matthew tells this scene. Shepherds in Israel often grazed sheep and goats together and parted them when needed. Every hearer had seen it done. The right hand was the place of honour; when Solomon's mother came to him, he had a throne set for her “at his right hand” (1 Kings 2:19).

The deeds on the list were not new ideas. They were the heart of Jewish piety. Isaiah said the fast God wants is “to share your bread with the hungry, to bring the poor and homeless into your home, to clothe the naked when you see him” (Isaiah 58:7). Ezekiel described a righteous man as one who “gives his bread to the hungry and covers the naked with clothing” (Ezekiel 18:7). What is startling is not the list. It is who receives the help. The King says the hungry man was him.

Prison in that world was usually a place to hold someone before trial or punishment. Prisoners often depended on family and friends for food and clothing. Visiting them was a lifeline, and it could be risky to be seen with them. The early Christians took this passage seriously. In the second century the satirist Lucian, who wrote in Greek and mocked Christians, described how they crowded to the prison every day with meals for a man they thought was one of their own (The Passing of Peregrinus 12).

The passage has shaped Christian charity for centuries. An early story about Martin, a Roman soldier who later became a bishop in Gaul, tells how at the gate of the city of Amiens he cut his military cloak in two with his sword and gave half to a poor man with almost no clothes. That night, the story says, he saw Christ in a dream wearing the half he had given away (Sulpicius Severus, Life of Martin 3).
passages.ot:
The scene draws on Daniel's vision of “One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven,” who is given a kingdom so “that the people of every nation and language should serve Him” (Daniel 7:13-14).

The shepherd who judges between his animals comes from Ezekiel, where God says to his flock, “I will judge between one sheep and another, between the rams and the goats” (Ezekiel 34:17). In the same chapter God promises to set one shepherd over them, his servant David. Here Jesus is both: the shepherd and the King.

Proverbs had already said that what is done for the poor is done to God: “Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD” (Proverbs 19:17).
passages.hard:
Who are ‘the least of these brothers of Mine’? Christians read this in two main ways, and both have careful defenders.

Some hold that the least are Jesus' followers, especially his messengers sent out in need. In Matthew Jesus calls his disciples his brothers: “Here are My mother and My brothers” (12:49), and after he rises, “Go and tell My brothers” (28:10). He had told them, “He who receives you receives Me” (10:40), and promised a reward to anyone who gives “a cup of cold water to one of these little ones because he is My disciple” (10:42). On this reading the nations are judged by how they treated Christ's people. A history of how the passage has been read (Sherman Gray, 1989) found that before modern times most writers took the least to be Christians.

Others hold that the least are all who suffer, believers or not. They point out that the list of needs is universal, that all the nations are gathered, and that the righteous are surprised, which would be odd if they knew they were helping Christians. They point to Jesus' command to love even enemies (5:44) and to the good Samaritan, who helped a stranger (Luke 10:25-37). Many churches today teach this reading.

These notes do not choose between them. On both readings, care for the hungry, the stranger, the sick and the prisoner is a mark of those who belong to the King. And on both, Christ stands with the weak so closely that what is done to them is done to him.

The scene gathers ‘all the nations’, but notice that the King separates people ‘one from another’. It is not a verdict on any country or any people as a whole. Each person stands before him.
passages.asks: Neither the sheep nor the goats knew whom they were meeting. The righteous did not help the hungry to earn a reward. They simply helped. Ask who in your week is hungry, lonely, new in town, sick or locked away. Ask whether you have met Christ there without knowing it. And ask whose door you have walked past.

passages.t: “You did not do for Me”: eternal punishment and eternal life
passages.happening:
Then the King turns to those on his left. “Depart from Me, you who are cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (verse 41). The list comes again, this time as what they did not do. I was hungry and you gave me nothing to eat. I was a stranger and you did not take me in. I was sick and in prison and you did not visit me.

They are as surprised as the others. ‘Lord, when did we see You hungry or thirsty or a stranger or naked or sick or in prison, and did not minister to You?’ The King answers, “Truly I tell you, whatever you did not do for one of the least of these, you did not do for Me” (verse 45).

The scene ends in one sentence: “And they will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (verse 46). With that, Jesus' last long teaching in Matthew is over.
passages.hearers:
Notice what the people on the left are judged for. Not for cruelty. Not for some terrible crime. For what they did not do. They walked past. In the parable of the talents the third servant also did nothing. Both stories warn against a safe, careful life that never gives itself away.

Notice too a difference in the King's words. The kingdom was prepared ‘for you’, for the righteous, from the foundation of the world (verse 34). The fire was prepared ‘for the devil and his angels’ (verse 41). Jesus does not say it was made for human beings. Many readers have seen in this that God's purpose for people is the kingdom, and that judgment is not what he made them for.

Many Jews of Jesus' day expected God to raise the dead at the end of time and to judge the world. Jesus speaks inside that hope, and he places himself at its centre: he is the judge.

This scene ends the fifth and last of the long teachings in Matthew. The next verse begins, “When Jesus had finished saying all these things” (26:1), and the story turns to his death.
passages.ot:
The two endings of verse 46 echo Daniel, one of the plainest Old Testament passages about the dead being raised to two different ends: “And many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt” (Daniel 12:2).

The Old Testament also says plainly that to ignore the poor is to sin against God. “Whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor, he too shall cry out and receive no answer” (Proverbs 21:13).
passages.hard:
Does this passage teach that people are saved by doing good deeds? There is no mention here of faith or grace. Christians have answered in more than one way. Many, following the Reformers, read the deeds as the fruit of a life already changed by grace, as a tree is known by its fruit (7:17). They point out that the righteous ‘inherit’ a kingdom ‘prepared’ for them, a gift and not a wage, and that they are surprised, so they were not counting their good deeds. Catholic teaching says that good works done in God's grace truly count before God, while grace is always their source. Paul's words hold both sides. “For it is by grace you have been saved through faith,” he writes, “not by works.” And in the next breath, we are “created in Christ Jesus to do good works” (Ephesians 2:8-10). James says faith without deeds is dead (James 2:17). Christians still differ in how they put these together. All agree that a faith that never feeds the hungry is not the faith Jesus recognises.

What is ‘eternal punishment’? Christians agree that Jesus warned of real and final judgment. They differ on its nature. The view most widely held through church history is that it is endless, conscious separation from God. Augustine argued that since verse 46 uses the same word ‘eternal’ for both punishment and life, if one is endless the other must be too (City of God 21.23). Others hold that the wicked will finally cease to exist, so the punishment is eternal in its result, not as endless suffering. Still others hope that God's love will in the end restore all people. These notes state the views and do not settle the question.

The warning is not meant to frighten anyone into faith, and it is not the whole picture. The same Jesus who warns is the one who says, “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest” (11:28). If you are afraid of God's judgment, hear that voice first. And within days of this speech the King himself will be the stranger, stripped and thirsty and condemned (27:28, 27:48), so that the door of the kingdom could be opened to people who were never worthy of it.
passages.asks: The people on the left were not accused of hating the poor. They simply did not see them. Ask what keeps you from seeing: busyness, fear, comfort, or the idea that someone else will help. Judgment in this scene is about whether love reached the people right in front of you. That is a question to carry into tomorrow, not to settle by reading.
